title: eCPRI: add dissector for IWF Start-Up (spec 2.0)
description:
Implemented dissector for IWF Start-Up message according to the
specification: https://www.cpri.info/downloads/eCPRI_v_2.0_2019_05_10c.pdf

Existing hf_* fields were renamed to match the message types to
better represent the expected layout of the dissected packet. 
Along with this change, most of the existing filters were 
reassigned to different values that follow the pattern "ecpri.x.y",
where 'x' is short name of the message type and 'y' is the 
particular field name.

The last change contains a few simplifications in the logic, where
multiple checks were done without any helper variables.

I'm not a fan of having structs with hf items inside them.  You have e.g., 'pc_id' fields in several structs, would it make sense to have a single (and therefore filterable) pc_id field that was used in every message that needs it?

Hello, thanks for the review! 

To be honest, I decided to take the `pc_id` (as well as `seq_id` and possibly some other fields) out of the "common fields", since in the eCPRI specification these are defined as: 

> "PC_ID: An identifier of a series of “IQ Data Transfer” messages"

> "PC_ID: An identifier of a series of “Bit Sequence Transfer” messages"

My understanding of "identifier of a series of XYZ messages" was that the PC_ID is distinguishable between various message types. Also, the allocation of PC_ID value is vendor specific, so each vendor could use some different strategy to allocate these values and maybe it would happen that the PC_ID was not common (just a guess)? After getting a bit deeper into the specification (sorry, this is my first time doing some implementation for Wireshark that makes use of such document) it seems that the PC_ID is actually a common field in various message sequence diagrams, meaning that I will change it.

I have a few questions about having structs though:

1. Why do you not like them? Coming to see such code without any structs for the first time might be a bit tedious, since the only documentation we have is comments and from my experience, it is fairly easy to forget about updating the comment.
2. What do you think about keeping structs in a way that I prepared them now, but with the changed filtering? This way we would have a clean code with structures (each message is distinguishable in the code and we do not need hfs such as `hf_element_id2`), but still the user would be able to filter out interesting data using `ecpri.pcid == ...` filter.

```c
{ &hf_iq_data.pc_id, { "PC_ID", "ecpri.pcid", FT_UINT16, BASE_HEX, NULL, 0x0, NULL, HFILL } },
{ &hf_bit_sequence.pc_id, { "PC_ID", "ecpri.pcid", FT_UINT16, BASE_HEX, NULL, 0x0, NULL, HFILL } },
{ &hf_generic_data_transfer.pc_id, { "PC_ID", "ecpri.pcid", FT_UINT32, BASE_HEX, NULL, 0x0, NULL, HFILL } },
{ &hf_iwf_start_up.pc_id, { "PC_ID", "ecpri.pcid", FT_UINT16, BASE_HEX, NULL, 0x0, NULL, HFILL } },
```
3. What fields, if any, other than PC_ID would you consider common? From what I see now, SEQ_ID is also used in 4 messages.

4. If the previous solution (with multiplied filters) is not a good one for you, what do you think about having some `common_ids_t` structure that would hold the data that is common among these messages? Or maybe these common fields could be outside any structure, so we could have common code inside the global scope as variables, but the other stuff that is inside messages would be packed in the structs?

I am open to any feedback and will happily align the code to what you propose.
+1 with Martin, not a big fan of struct, it is not on style of other dissector...
@martin.r.mathieson and @alagoutte, the code is now aligned as you mentioned, no structs are left for hf.

Hi Tomasz,

In terms of having unique fields for each message type, that is up to you and whatever makes sense for the protocol.  If there is really no linkage between (say) PC_ID or SEQ_ID as they appear in separate message types, I'm fine with them using separate fields. When typing in filter names, it is nice to be able to type 'ecpri.gtd.' and have the relevant fields appear. I don't really know this protocol (though I happen to work with ORAN FH CUS which is carried upon message types 0, and 2 - at some point I might become interested also in type 5).

However, I would still prefer to have a flat array of hf entries.  You can still order and group them by message type, e.g., you could have all of the hf entries share a common 'hf_common_header_' prefix, and group them together (in order of usage, with line breaks between message types if you prefer) when you declare and define them.

One (selfish) reason for preferring not to use the structs to group hf items is that I help maintain some checking scripts that would likely be confused by this dissector looking different from all of the others.

Hi Martin,

I fully understand why you prefer flat variables instead of structures now! Regarding the connection of PC_ID, SEQ_ID and the protocol. I am not really working with it (eCPRI), I was trying to find some protocol that had some dissector not fully aligned to the latest specification, as I am just trying to get into the Wireshark world by doing code, not just by reading it. My understanding of the specification is that these fields may be common, but it is not obvious, since it is still a vendor-specific information. In my code I have changed all PC_ID fields to contain the same filter `ecpri.pcid`, but in case anything needs the alignment in the future, I am happy to help.

If this answer and the code satisfies you, please mark this thread as resolved.
This is fine, if someone working with these fields finds it convenient they could decide to change it.

eCPRI: add dissector for IWF Start-Up (spec 2.0)

Implemented dissector for IWF Start-Up message according to the
specification: https://www.cpri.info/downloads/eCPRI_v_2.0_2019_05_10c.pdf

Existing hf_* fields were wrapped in simple structs in order to
show the expected layout of the dissected packet. Along with this
change, existing filters were reassigned to different values that
follow the pattern "ecpri.x.y", where 'x' is short name of the
message type and 'y' is the particular field name.

The last change contains a few simplifications in the logic, where
multiple checks were done without any helper variables.
